It also refines the picture by supplying the metrical…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper never states a stress rule of its own; it is a historical study of vowel shifts. What it carries about stress is (a) its report of Nercesian 2011b: Wichi words are parsed into iambic feet (weak-strong), the head of each iamb lengthens, and the foot-parsed forms it prints put primary stress on the last syllable of the root/word with secondary stress on the heads of preceding iambs, e.g. *(he.t’és) ‘fermented drink’, *(ke.tés) ‘star’, *(heɁ.yáx) ‘jaguar’, *(e.sì)(náx) ‘dog’ (p.28, ex. 27) and (ʔi.tɑ́x) ‘fire’, (la.pɑ̀)(sét) ‘lip’, (ta.kɑ̀)(lɑ́) ‘leg, foot’, (ʔɑ.n̥ɑ̀)(lɑ́) ‘vizcacha’ (p.47, ex. 43); (b) the statement that in pelhéy > pelháy the stress on the bound root moved to the plural suffix -ey, i.e. suffixation shifts stress to the new final syllable. Taken together: primary stress on the final syllable of the (suffixed) word, built by right-headed binary feet. Secondary reports of other authors in the same section: Viñas Urquiza 1974 (Misión Chaqueña) has a 'syllable with primary stress and tone 4 (emphasis)' that lengthens the vowel; Tovar 1981 (Embarcación/Tartagal/Misión La Paz) has an 'intensity stress, namely "affective or emphatic"', which lengthens the vowel with falling intonation; Najlis 1984 reconstructs Proto-Mataguayan stress as 'phonologically unpredictable (prefixes are unstressed, inflectional suffixes are stressed, and the stem is grave, with oxytone exceptions that generally result from compositions)' and says Wichi changed that pattern (p.20).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Shown by grave accents on the head of every non-final iamb in the foot-parsed forms: (si.wà:)(n̥á:s) ‘ant’, (la.qà:)(tiʰ.jè:n)(’nú:) ‘you make me jump’ (p.19); (e.sì)(náx) ‘dog’, (la.pɑ̀)(sét) ‘lip’, (ta.kɑ̀s)(lé) ‘guts’, (la.čɑ̀)(tí) ‘grandfather’, (ʔɑ.n̥ɑ̀)(lɑ́) ‘vizcacha’ (pp.28, 47). No prose rule for secondary stress is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None for placement as such. The paper notes (p.28, running [27]) that the /e/ that lowers is 'mostly in the light syllable of the iambic foot, unstressed and presumably short in all cases … except for some words (*ho.sén ‘axe’; *pe.ɬéy ‘storm, thunder’; …)', which concern the vowel change, not stress placement. It also relays that vowel length varies by geographic area and that emphatic/affective stress (Tovar, Viñas Urquiza) lengthens vowels; the end-note on historical orthographies (p.62) treats the acute in Remedi 1896/1904, Pelleschi 1887 and Lehmann-Nitsche 1910/1925 as marking 'lexical stress'.
new_statements.identity_note: The paper treats Wichi as a single language with two main present-day dialects, Pilcomayeño (upstream/central/downstream) and Bermejeño; the foot-parsed stress examples come from Nercesian 2011b/2014a, whose data are Wichi 'spoken downstream of the Bermejo River, in the province of Formosa' (Bermejeño), not the Pilcomayo Güisnay lect (wich1264) the catalog names. The other stress remarks it relays are localized: Viñas Urquiza 1970/1974 = Misión Chaqueña (Salta, Central Pilcomayeño); Tovar 1981 = Embarcación, Tartagal and Misión La Paz (Salta); Terraza 2009 = Rivadavia Banda Sur (Salta); Claesson 1994/2016 = Upstream Pilcomayeño (Bolivian Weenhayek/Noctén).

readall_conflicts: The one opened work (Nercesian & Arellano 2024) presents Wichi word stress as iambic with primary stress on the final syllable of the (suffixed) word and secondary stress on preceding foot heads, following Nercesian 2011b; this disagrees with the catalog's coded fixed: initial syllable pattern for wich1264, which the catalog's own check already traces to an StressTyp2 English interpolation ('on the first syllable') absent from the Spanish of Viñas Urquiza 1974:32. The paper's sources also disagree among themselves on domain and predictability, as the catalog notes: it relays Tovar 1981's 'affective or emphatic' intensity stress and Viñas Urquiza 1974's emphasis-conditioned 'primary stress and tone 4', while Najlis 1984 reconstructs Proto-Mataguayan stress as phonologically unpredictable with paroxytone stems and stressed inflectional suffixes and says Wichi changed that pattern. The 2024 paper does not resolve the word-versus-phrase question; it simply uses word-level iambic parses.

audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant FINAL (final stress), non-strict, citing Avram 2008:79-80 (Misión La Paz, on-target lect: ultimate stress at 2, 3, 4 syllables) as deciding source, with Viñas Urquiza 1974:32 (displacement to final syllable under suffixation) and Nercesian 2011:81 / 2014:80 (Bermejo: primary stress on head of rightmost iambic foot; 'suelen tener el acento en la última sílaba') as corroboration, and a caution line for Tovar 1981:172 / Hunt 1940:9 (position varies with phrase rhythm) and Claesson 1994:6 (Noctén: free stress). Alternatively 'undetermined' if the catalog register requires an on-target source stronger than an MA thesis; in no case initial.
audit.deciding_source_kind: database or survey citing another work
audit.reasoning: The live kind/rule (fixed initial) is StressTyp2's coding, and every primary text opened contradicts it: the Spanish that StressTyp2 itself quotes from Viñas Urquiza 1974:32 puts primary stress on the final syllable under suffixation (StressTyp2's 'first syllable' is an added gloss); Avram 2008:79-80, the only phonological description of the Güisnay/Pilcomayo lect (held, verified verbatim), states ultimate stress; Nercesian 2011 (held) and the Nercesian 2014 Manual downloaded now (p.80, p.162) give final stress for the Bermejo variety; Tovar 1981:172 (held) says phrase rhythm. The record's own editor note already concludes fixed: initial syllable survives under no reading, yet the kind/rule fields still carry initial stress. Quotations in the domain quotation/sources are all confirmed in copies we hold, so the problem is the classification, not the evidence: reclassify as fixed: final syllable (dominant) on Avram 2008 with Viñas Urquiza/Nercesian corroboration

tone.quote: Two phenomena should be distinguished in Wichí at the suprasegmental level: vowel length (symbolized here with the acute accent) and stress (marked with the sign ˈ). The distribution of the vowel length (§9.1.3.1) follows a complex left-aligned pattern, with different morphemes (including lexical roots) having different underlying specifications; in Chapter 4 we argued that this pattern is the direct continuation of the Proto-Mataguayan accent. ’Weenhayek is the only variety known to systematically preserve the vowel length distinctions of Proto-Wichí. By contrast, the stress (§9.1.3.2) is right-aligned in Wichí, its function is to signal the right edge of the word, and the only complication is that a few suffixes are specified as extrametrical.
tone.locator: p.406, §9.1.3 'Word-level prosody' (ch.9 Wichí); see also p.410 §9.1.3.2 and p.465 §9.2.3 (Misión La Paz)
tone.summary: No tone: word prosody = right-edge (final) stress with lexically extrametrical suffixes (then penult) + inherited contrastive vowel length surviving only in ’Weenhayek; secondary stress iambic L-to-R (documented for Lower Bermejeño only).

[...] [p.228] en la variedad del Pilcomayo que estudiamos, la fluctuación (en el mismo hablante) o la alternancia (en hablantes y comunidades distintas) /h/ + /n/ ocurre con /h/ y no con /n/ como señala Viñas Urquiza.
